title: Origins and History of Lighthouse (Fresnel)
body:
The Lighthouse (Fresnel) belongs to the 1820s–present era and traces to Various.

Sail ruled for millennia; the clipper ship (1840s–60s, e.g., Flying Cloud's 89-day New York–San Francisco run) was sail's apex. Steam auxiliaries became steam primaries: paddle wheels gave way to screws; iron and steel replaced wood. The ocean liner era (Mauretania 1907, Titanic 1912, Queen Mary 1936, United States 1952) made the Atlantic a highway. Lighthouses (Fresnel lenses, 1820s) and lightships guarded coasts; the Coast Guard's cutters patrolled. Submarines (Holland, 1900) went from novelty to weapon. Containers (1956) ended the break-bulk age — and the liner era with it.

Within that longer story, Lighthouse (Fresnel): The 1820s; the 1900s'. The Fresnel is the light's lens.

title: How Lighthouse (Fresnel) Works
body:
Sailing ships trade wind for way: square rig runs before the wind, fore-and-aft rig points closer; hull speed (~1.34 × sqrt(waterline length)) caps displacement hulls. Steam plants (Scotch boilers, triple-expansion engines, then turbines) drove paddles then screws. Navigation was celestial + dead reckoning + lead line; lighthouses gave light characteristics (flash patterns) for landfall. Submarines dive by flooding ballast tanks and surface by blowing them; early boats ran on the surface with diesels (or gasoline!) and submerged on batteries.

Applied to the Lighthouse (Fresnel) (1820s–present, Various): The Fresnel is the light's lens.

The engineering principles above are exactly what made this class of technology practical: every unit is a working compromise between materials, energy, precision, and cost.

title: Lighthouse (Fresnel) — Hull speed + celestial fix helper (Runnable Python)
body:
Computes hull speed, passage times, and great-circle distances — the voyage-planning math of the sailing and steam eras.

The program below is real, runnable Python 3. Save it as demo.py and run `python3 demo.py`. It models the core mathematics of the Lighthouse (Fresnel) so you can experiment with the parameters yourself.
code:
# Maritime math: hull speed, passages, great circle (public-domain formulas)
import math

def hull_speed_kn(lwl_ft):
    return 1.34 * math.sqrt(lwl_ft)

for ship, lwl in [("clipper (200ft WL)", 200), ("liner (800ft WL)", 800),
                  ("sloop (25ft WL)", 25)]:
    print(f"{ship}: hull speed {hull_speed_kn(lwl):.1f} kn")

def nm_between(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
    # haversine, nautical miles
    r = 3440.065
    p1, p2 = math.radians(lat1), math.radians(lat2)
    dp, dl = p2 - p1, math.radians(lon2 - lon1)
    a = math.sin(dp/2)**2 + math.cos(p1)*math.cos(p2)*math.sin(dl/2)**2
    return 2 * r * math.asin(math.sqrt(a))

d = nm_between(40.7, -74.0, 51.5, -0.1)  # NY to London
print(f"\nNew York to London: {d:.0f} nm")
print(f"  at 12 kn (liner): {d/12/24:.1f} days ; at 6 kn (clipper avg): {d/6/24:.1f} days")
